idiom_name: nil checks with for-range loops, optionally factored into hand-written generic helpers
implementation_notes: Go deliberately has no Option type: absence is modelled with nil (pointer, map, slice, interface) plus comma-ok forms, and the standard slices package ships no Map/Filter/Reduce helpers, so a traversal is an explicit range loop with a nil check per element. Since Go 1.18 a generic helper such as FilterMap[T, U] can be written once and reused, which is the closest equivalent of a reusable traversal; otherwise the classic first-class accessor is replaced by the plain loop. Keep the loop when the code is local, and factor the helper only when the same traversal recurs.
pitfalls: A typed nil inside an interface does not equal nil, so an interface nil check can pass while the underlying pointer is nil.
range copies each element: assigning to the loop variable does not update the slice, and a struct element must be written back through the index or a pointer.
Traversal does not make access safe: concurrently ranging a slice or map that another goroutine mutates is a data race, and maps need their own synchronization.
